discrepancy: WebFetch refused (provenance). One WebSearch did not surface the athenum post, so the Binance/Bybit funding-history coverage was not checked.

label: IREF 2024
claim: Deprez and Frömmel's out-of-sample gains came from *portfolios* of rules chosen after costs, not from a single optimized rule ([IREF 2024]).
discrepancy: WebFetch refused (provenance). One WebSearch did not return this IDEAS record or the publisher page, so the portfolio-of-rules-after-costs finding was not checked.

label: arXiv 2606.00071
claim: Simpler models consistently beat complex ones out-of-sample in BTC ([arXiv 2606.00071]).
evidence: Survey says evidence is mixed: e.g. Gradojevic et al. (2023) Random Forest beat random walk; Magner & Hardy AR models beat RW for some coins; BTC naive-dominance result is one unreplicated preprint.
discrepancy: Source does not say simpler models 'consistently' beat complex ones for BTC; it explicitly describes non-uniform evidence and flags the BTC-specific result as unreplicated.

label: NBER w20592
claim: Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue that a new factor needs a **t-ratio above 3.0, not 2.0**, and that most claimed findings are likely false ([NBER w20592]).
evidence: "a t-ratio greater than 3.0"; "most claimed research findings in financial economics are likely false."
discrepancy: Abstract does not state '2.0' explicitly, but 2.0 is the conventional cutoff it argues against. Fetched the RePEc listing of NBER w20592.

label: Bailey & López de Prado
claim: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio adjusts a backtest Sharpe for the number of trials and for fat tails ([Bailey & López de Prado]).
evidence: DSR corrects for "selection bias under multiple testing" and non-normally distributed returns (title: "...Non-Normality").
discrepancy: Abstract says non-normality, not 'fat tails' specifically; equivalent in substance. Fetched after URL resurfaced via WebSearch.

label: Bailey et al.
claim: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting estimates, via combinatorial cross-validation, how often the in-sample winner underperforms out of sample ([Bailey et al.]), and an R implementation exists ([CRAN pbo]).
evidence: PBO estimated via "combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV)".
discrepancy: The abstract page confirms CSCV but does not define PBO as how often the in-sample winner underperforms out of sample. That definition was not verifiable from the fetched page.

label: CRAN pbo
claim: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting estimates, via combinatorial cross-validation, how often the in-sample winner underperforms out of sample ([Bailey et al.]), and an R implementation exists ([CRAN pbo]).
evidence: Vignette for R package 'pbo': computes probability of backtest overfitting, performance degradation, stochastic dominance; credits Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, Zhu.
discrepancy: URL is a CRAN mirror (FAU), not cran.r-project.org.

label: The Block citing Kaiko
claim: The post-ETF period from January 2024 to the present should be a final holdout opened once: volume has shifted toward US weekday hours since the ETFs ([The Block citing Kaiko]), and that is the regime the strategy will trade in.
evidence: Weekend share 16% (vs up to 28% in 2019); 3-4pm NY fixing window now second most popular trading time, weekdays only.
discrepancy: Kaiko attributes the decline only partly to ETFs (also cites bank closures). Holdout-design recommendation is the survey's own.

label: Concretum guide
claim: If an altcoin sleeve is ever revisited, the data must include delisted coins, or the backtest inherits the equal-weighted survivorship bias of tens of percent a year described above ([Concretum guide]).
evidence: Aims to avoid survivorship bias "by including both active and defunct projects"; ~23,286 coins.
discrepancy: Guide does not quantify survivorship bias; no 'tens of percent a year' or equal-weighted figure. That magnitude must come from another source.

label: Hedgeweek
claim: Crypto hedge funds returned about **40% in 2024 against roughly 120% for BTC** ([Hedgeweek]).
evidence: VisionTrack Composite (130 crypto hedge funds) up 40% in 2024; bitcoin up 120%.

label: Opalesque
claim: Their typical value has been smaller drawdowns, such as −46% against about −72% for BTC in 2018 ([Opalesque]).
evidence: PwC survey: median crypto hedge fund -46% in 2018; "Bitcoin down -72%."
discrepancy: Figures are calendar-year 2018 returns (median fund), not drawdowns as the claim states. They come from a PwC/Elwood survey relayed by Opalesque.

label: BIS Bulletin 69
claim: BIS found most crypto-app users lost money on BTC, largely by buying after rallies ([BIS Bulletin 69]), and a pre-committed rule guards against that behaviour even when it adds no alpha.
evidence: "a majority of crypto app users in nearly all economies made losses"; users "attracted by high prices" (PDF); median loss $431 of $900.
discrepancy: Losses are simulation-based estimates ('probably'). Buy-after-rally mechanism stated in the bulletin PDF (bis.org/publ/bisbull69.pdf), not the HTML summary.
